reasons: [coverage/major] D1 [criteriaAssessments C4; CL5, CL9, CL10; verdict; practicalImplications step 3] The legal analysis of the recommended Berlin 07:00-19:00 12-hour shift only checks the ArbZG night window (s.2) and the 11-hour rest rule (s.5). It leaves out the daily maximum working time in ArbZG s.3 (8 h, extendable to 10 h) and the Sunday and public-holiday work ban in ArbZG s.9-10. Under follow-the-sun, a Berlin engineer works a normal day and is also on call 07:00-19:00, every day of their on-call week including Saturday and Sunday. Call-outs at 07:00-09:00 or 17:00-19:00 count as working time and can push the day past 10 h. Any weekend or holiday call-out is Sunday or holiday work, which needs a statutory exception. The request asks for 'anything that could block or complicate the rollout', and the verdict calls the Berlin shift legally clean because it 'sits entirely outside the statutory night window'. That framing leaves out a plausible complication, and possibly a blocker, for the recommended design. The packet does not research it either, so the gap was not flagged.

[decision_usefulness/major] D2 [verdict (Step 2/Step 3 wording) vs practicalImplications step 3 and step 5] The verdict and the rollout steps disagree on when works council approval comes. The verdict says 'Step 2: run a time-boxed pilot... Step 3: confirm it only after the works council agrees', which implies the pilot can start before approval. practicalImplications step 5 says the pilot starts 'after approval'. HR notes (E5) and BetrVG s.87 (E15) say any change to the Berlin on-call schedule, a pilot included, needs works council approval first. A reader of the verdict alone could start an unlawful pilot in Berlin.

[coverage/major] D3 [criteriaAssessments C1, C3; CL7, CL8; K12-K14, K23-K24] C1 covers 'night-time and out-of-hours interruptions', but the draft only analyses the local-night window (22:00-06:00). Under the recommended split, SF is on call until 22:00 local on every on-call day, which covers the evening 18:00-22:00. Berlin covers 07:00-09:00 and 17:00-19:00 outside normal hours. Both offices also cover full 12-hour weekend days. The fairness comparison (CL7: 16.8 h vs 21 h vs 18.7 h today) treats business-hours on-call time the same as out-of-hours time. That makes the comparison apples-to-oranges: much of a 12-hour daytime shift overlaps normal working hours and costs far less than 24/7 hours. The draft does not quantify out-of-hours or weekend on-call hours per person per office, which is the metric that actually matters for burnout and fairness.

[alternatives_counterarguments/major] D4 [alternatives; counterarguments[0]; criteriaAssessments C1/C5] Option (a) is never assessed together with noise tuning. The alternatives list contains '(a) with no noise tuning', '(b) with no noise tuning', 'noise removal only' and 'hybrid = tuning + (b)'. The recommended hybrid therefore gets credit for tuning (1.1 pages per shift) that option (a) would get too. The fair comparison is (a)+tuning vs (b)+tuning, and it is missing. The counterargument response on (a) ('after tuning, load is about 2.3 pages a day') quietly uses tuning against (a) without scoring (a)+tuning. Variants of (a) are also not considered, such as a secondary in the opposite office who takes the primary's local-night pages. That variant would answer C1 without 12-hour shifts.

[reasoning_validity/major] D1 [verdict; criteriaAssessments C1 (assessment, strengths), C3; CL18, CL19; alternatives 'Option (a) with noise tuning' and 'Recommended hybrid'; counterargument[0]; K31, K32, K36] The new out-of-hours comparison counts secondary standby hours the same as primary hours for option (a), and then sets that against follow-the-sun with no secondary. K31 (2*(168-40)/9 = 28.44 h), K32 (12.44 local-night h) and K36 (10.67 weekend h) all double the primary figure because a secondary is added. A secondary is only paged on escalation, so it carries far less interruption load than a primary. The draft itself says how often the secondary would be paged is unknown (E12 limitations). The draft's own rollout also allows a daytime secondary within follow-the-sun, so the comparison does not hold like for like. Even so, the 28.4 h vs 9.8-11 h gap is used as a main argument: the verdict, C1 strengths, alternatives ('less than half the out-of-hours load per person'), and the first counterargument response. The fairer like-for-like figure is the primary-only 14.2 h (K30) vs 9.8-11 h. That gap is still real but much smaller (about 23-31% lower). The ranking probably survives on the zero-local-night point, but the size of the out-of-hours advantage is overstated.

[minor/reviewer] D1 [verdict ('Saturday included'); criteriaAssessments C4 assessment; edgeCasesAndFailureModes item 5 ('full 8-hour working day (Mon-Sat)'); rollout step 3 ('Berlin on-call working days (Mon-Sat)')] The text that was changed to fix the Saturday/s.9 problem now overreaches the other way. The verdict says call-outs 'on top of a normal working day, Saturday included, may exceed the s.3 daily ceiling'. C4 says 'On working days (Mon-Sat), call-outs on top of a normal 8-hour day could exceed the s.3 ceiling'. The draft's own working-hours assumption is 09:00-17:00 on weekdays only (K25-K30), so a Berlin engineer has no normal 8-hour day on Saturday. The 8 h + more than 2 h call-out breach scenario therefore applies Monday to Friday. On Saturday, s.3 is reached only by call-outs alone. The correct legal point is that s.3 covers Saturday and s.9 does not. Saying that Saturday call-outs sit on top of a normal workday overstates the Saturday s.3 risk.
